utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue. Just a second. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Before we begin, I'd like to introduce Ms. Marlene Yahya Haage, who will be assisting me this morning, who is sitting here to my right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn it up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you hear me well, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. The others have heard me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, last week we discussed the ways of waging war. Did the warring parties use ruses, tricks and perfidies and did you witness that, were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly these things happened. As for perfidy, I have no information and I was not able to assess that units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps used that. And when we talk about certain tricks and frame-ups, in my case and my reporting that would refer to the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And I do not include in that certain military cunning that is normal and allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate to us the distinction between military ruses that are allowed under international law and those that are not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly very clear, and when I say "legitimate military ruses," I mean surprise attacks, attempts by the enemy to disguise his axes of movement, mask his intentions and the actions he intends to mount, that is not only allowed, that is necessary. However, speaking of illegitimate actions, it boils down to illegitimate action against civilians and facilities and installations that have nothing to do with military purposes, not only buildings but also land. So I believe wilful and disproportionate action to be not allowed, illegitimate, as well as any irregular attitude towards civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last week you mentioned provocations that were meant to elicit our response. In which category would you place action, such action, from hospitals, from places close to UN forces' bases, et cetera, would you qualify that as legitimate or illegitimate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is unequivocal and obvious. To open fire from hospitals, from rehabilitation centres and similar places, from areas inhabited by civilian population, hoping that fire would not be returned would certainly be illegitimate and perfidious, also if it is calculated to provoke return and very damaging fire by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As commander and as a military unit, was it your interest to engage in such provocations yourself and to engage them in combat from such areas, in political media terms?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commitment of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its command and its key commanding officers and the entire military structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was not to provoke or engage in any action, just to portray ourselves as being threatened in an illegitimate way. The entire structure of the SRK, and especially the command and brigade commanders, were only interested in military solutions on the battle-field between the warring parties. And we had strictly to adhere to that so that the entire course of military actions and the image it would create -- we had to be, in other words, seen to be doing that in a chivalrous manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslim side succeed in cashing in in the media and politically speaking on all those incidents when you did return fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would call it superfluous and going over the top, creating the impression that the Muslim side is threatened. Of course the civilian population would certainly be threatened as a result of our action, opening fire, carelessness, et cetera. I think they worked hard to create that impression with major assistance provided by certain players, but I don't want to go into that now. They did a lot to create the image that they are threatened as a result of our irregular action and pressure against the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the nature of that conduct, their actions which were not aimed at making a breakthrough but at provoking return fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that the corps command and our personnel were perfectly aware of what was going on and what aims the enemy is pursuing and what they want to blame the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for. In this respect we were united and there was no problem amongst us to agree on that assessment and to adhere to that assessment and to agree on a conduct that would prevent them from creating the wrong impression about us. Of course that was not easy. It was not easy to resist that propaganda and their attempts to create an atmosphere in which we would look as if we were engaging in irregular action, irregular conduct, which would not be soldierly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In such cases, when you put up with fire opened at you from hospitals, civilian buildings, and other facilities that should not be used for military purposes, what did you do? In what cases did you have to just take it and in what cases did you have to return fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position and the assessment I described before to the extent that my command and myself and my subordinated commanders were aware of it, aware of those attempts to set us up, we could not just make that assessment once and for all. We had to continuously review the situation on a case-by-case basis, based on all the information we had collected. I have to explain in my own way that within the system of deployment of forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps we had developed a system of observation. That system of observation is something that you absolutely must have when you are facing the enemy. We had separate observers for artillery fire, observers of infantry action, movements and manoeuvre, and of course there were, generally speaking, observers of air-space but that was not relevant for us. This observer structure provided us at each and every moment with information about what was going on, what was happening, what intentions are beginning to take shape, what is apparently in the offing, et cetera, and that information would reach the commanding officer, who would then make his assessment. Usually the commanding officer would have to verify, although the observer was a trained observer, the commanding officer would have to make his own assessment whether this information is correct and reliable, whether the area concerned is a clearing with only one combat vehicle opening fire or it is an area that is a populated area where fire would cause damage to civilian situations -- civilian population. There were situations that were perfectly obvious and clear. If, for instance, we saw a building with lots of sandbags on the balcony and a machine-gun nest between the sandbags, it did not require a lot of assessment to decide whether that was a target that needed to be neutralised or a target that could result in collateral civilian damage. We concluded that if fire is opened from such bunkers on balconies, that had nothing to do with the civilian structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D7503, a regular combat report containing some of those things you just described related to anticipation and expectations. 1D7503. This is a regular combat report dated 8 December 1993. Could we look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could you present to us item 8. What does it refer to? Could we see the previous page in English, item 8.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What do I say on my part, not just pertaining to the document but in general? These were such attempts to portray us as the side seeking for the right moment to disturb life in Sarajevo in general, especially the work of civilian organs, et cetera. Forecasts were made. There was a conclusion and appropriate regulation was identified in order to address specific events. When we believed that there would be an attempt to make a move which would then shift the blame onto our side, we tried to forecast such problems, issue warnings, and our ranks acted in line with our proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your proposals, General? You said "in line with our proposals." What are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proposals and instructions, Your Honour. There were specific instructions issued to the units on how to address specific situations. The first item was that it was to be expected that certain provocations would take place which amounted to nothing basically and that our reaction to such provocations should not be provoked. The proposal was to -- well, I'd say not to get us involved, to engage in certain actions which would be impermissible, whereas the incident was merely a provocation. There were such forecasts made that similar situations may occur and that we should bear in mind that our actions should not be provoked as to portray it as illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what does this pertain to? It says the following: "The decision remains intact or unchanged." We'll see another document --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision for further action is unchanged. These had been our previous position. So we had to make sure that we were not provoked, that such provocations would be avoided in order to avoid creating problems for our side. All of the regulation positions were in place pertaining to specific situations. We always strove to avoid acting upon any incidents in cases where it would be impermissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 1D1641, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is your regular combat report as deputy commander dated the 9th of January, 1994. Item 3(a), please. "At around 0900 hours, a 120-millimetre shell fell on the Sarajevo airport. It occurred as the airplane with Mr. Akashi was being awaited." And then we have Mr. Akashi's visit to Pale the next day referred to. What does this refer to? It certainly was something that was expected to take place during Ambassador Akashi's visit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly shows that there was an attempt to make use of Mr. Akashi's arrival, to cause an incident which would then be blamed on the Serbian side to show that the Serbian side did not honour any of its agreements. It included international elements and the fact that the airport had been handed over to the international community. They were trying to get an indication that our side would seize such opportunities when prominent persons came to engage in action. We believed that the enemy was prepared to try and impose such scenarios on our side and that we should not be provoked under any circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us how successful was the other side in order to tarnish the image of our side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always tried to show the international community that such things, seeking to provoke us or such UNPROFOR activities which shifted -- which seemed to shift the blame on our side, that it was not the case, especially if the international community was supposed to act as mediator. We always strove to show that such were not our intentions and our actions. I'm glad to say that it was never successful on the side of the other party. I don't think such assessments were finally made on the Serbian side -- about the Serbian side. Perhaps I can use an example. General Gobillard arrived in my command, claiming that we had destroyed a house at Sedrenik when we used excessive force allegedly. I took note of what he said and I simply had to see it for myself. My commanders and fighters told me that the house was full of sandbags and the balcony simply fell through, taking parts of the wall with it because of the weight. And then it was reported that our side brought the building down. I indeed saw numerous sandbags and that this was no result of any action on our part. I conveyed that information to General Gobillard, but it was my feeling that he didn't believe me. We always had to investigate and study, we always had to check whether UNPROFOR information was correct. And I always tried to influence my men to simply exclude any such possibilities of similar action. We couldn't get rid of it easily, though, because we were constantly being put in situations whereby we were portrayed as the unfair side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, what kind of route did you have to traverse as the corps command from your command post to Sedrenik, to verify General Gobillard's allegations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand the question, but the route was not an issue for me, although I understand the thrust of the question. I'm trying to convey something else, that there were attempts to do away with this sort of anathema that was being imposed on the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as the side which wages war unfairly. I will try to answer. So in short I had to cross over 50 kilometres, but it was an aside for me. There were numerous other occasions when I went to the location where I had to clear things up with UNPROFOR commanders or with the people on my side who may have engaged in something inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a strictly confidential report to the Main Staff, or rather, to the forward command post. In item 3(a) it is stated that the landing of 27 planes is planned for today, four planes have landed, and Izetbegovic and Franjo Kuharic flew out of Sarajevo. Did you envisage any alternative in case the Trebevic-Sarajevo road was closed off for Mr. Akashi to be able to use it? How could that take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a separate issue. As far as I recall, I have explained some of that already here. There were several routes which were chosen as a powerful force from Sarajevo to threaten our positions or our axes. There was the route Sarajevo-Lukavica and Pale via Trebevic. It was one particular area that they attacked incessantly with all their might, trying to cut it off. That was the basic axis. I do realise that additional routes had to be chosen which would take one the roundabout way and it required construction machinery to clear off parts of such routes in order to secure communication between Lukavica and Pale via Trebevic should the original route be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D1649, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're going to stay with the topic, General. Could you discuss item 8 for the benefit of the Chamber and the participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the text speaks for itself in item 8. It was our decision that our further action remain unchanged. We pursued the same line according to the same principles and regulations, in order to create conditions, to further honour what had been decided earlier in terms of principles and regulations to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe everyone can see from the document that there were no problems with UNPROFOR and the convoys.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document admitted? It is of the 23rd of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Correct? Can we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the day before this document, did your forces open artillery or mortar fire Alipasino Polje, and if you recall -- well, on the 22nd of January, one day previously, did your forces open fire on Alipasino Polje from heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think maybe we need some agreement on what constitutes a leading question. When you say: Did your forces open fire on Alipasino Polje from heavy artillery, that can be equally answered yes or no, it doesn't suggest an answer. It is my understanding of a leading question is a question that suggests the answer, so I don't understand how that question is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Tieger, instead of Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, only because I think this will involve any number of questions and answers and witnesses over the course of time, and I think Mr. Robinson is aware that it's context-based. Information can be conveyed in the context of a question that's framed yes or no that provides the critical information at issue. So it depends on the nature of the question. If where in a particular context fire was or shelling was made and that information is provided, then the leading nature of the question is manifest. So the answer is not simply going to be the precise way -- whether or not the question is technically framed as a yes-or-no question, but the nature of the information that's being conveyed. I think that's a fair assessment and I know -- I can try to find it - that in a previous situation Judge Morrison made that precise point to one of the examiners and I don't even remember whether it was a Prosecution or a Defence examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if it had been a leading question, he didn't succeed. The witness answered he doesn't know. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question as formulated in -- and with the specific date included has element of leading question. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. I will reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd or the 23rd, did you receive a protest from the United Nations? And if that was the case, would that have been contained in your reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had received it, I would have included it. I can't say whether I received a protest. I can't say whether there was anything going on in Alipasino Polje. This is my answer. If a protest had been received, we would have checked the situation, and in this case, as I sit here today, I really don't remember any such thing. I don't remember that that happened. I know that we did not do anything that was not allowed and that we did not open fire inhabited by the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2806, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, during your checks on that time or around that time, did you establish that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had opened fire on Alipasino Polje and caused some unlawful damage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever checks I carried out, whatever attempts I made to establish the truth, i.e., whether fire was opened and how it was opened after the warnings that there were illegalities involved in the fire opening, I would check that. I went all the way to the place where the crews were, those crews and those combatants that were in the sector. I wanted to gain accurate information from them relying on the trust that existed between me and them. At any given moment they could confide in me as to what had been done. I never received an answer to the effect that they were arrogant in what they were doing, that they opened fire on the people that they should not have opened fire on. During my checks I used several methods. I talked to the officers. I talked to the combatants, to the observers, and I never received any information to the effect that irregularities had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I call up D1515. This is a Defence exhibit, D1515.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please look at the bottom where it says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up a little? Could we go to the bottom of the page. I believe that in English it should be on the following page, the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read what you did regarding the alleged fire being opened on Dobrinja on the 4th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In connection with the allegation, I have to say that whenever information was provided we had to check it. We received information that an 82-millimetre shell was launched, but we did not want to take that for granted. In order to verify the information we checked what had happened. I didn't do it myself. That was done by Colonel Kosovac. He obtained information that no such fire had been opened, i.e., that that was refuted in the Republika Srpska media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the last sentence it says: "The Jewish convoy and activities in this respect are proceeding according to plan." Do you remember that convoy? I had negotiated that in New York. One of the witnesses put these two events in relation. Did you notice that there was a link between these two events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm aware of those events. Let's be clear on one thing. I don't know how the decision on the convoy of Jews was arrived at. I know what happened next, that their request was met, our factors were involved in that, and those people were allowed to leave Sarajevo according to plan and according to their wishes. However, obviously I -- I'm trying to establish a link here. The idea was to say this: You agree to something and then we will -- you would manipulate things in order to make the whole thing pointless, i.e., to blame us for hindering the departure of the Jewish community from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 1D7513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell us what actions and what preparations you undertook in order to -- you say here that on the 4th of February, 1994, you carried out certain activities. What did the corps do? Did the corps carry out operations to prepare themselves for an offensive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we did not prepare an offensive. We were preparing ourselves for defence. When you say "offensive," I translate that into attacks on our part, but that's not the only thing that I want to say. Furthermore, here I can see bullet point 2, where it says: "To build and improve the basic defence positions. "To build the reserve defence positions. "To build the false defence positions. "And protect all the shelters ..." and so on and so forth. This is a period during which General Rose made it possible -- or at least that's how I perceived the whole situation. He was the one who made sure that there was a cease-fire between the two warring parties and I congratulate him on that. What I'm trying to say here is that during that period of time, a cease-fire was in place and a cease of all hostilities, which means that we did not open any fire at that time. We were reinforcing our positions. We did not have any other plans. We did not open fire. We did not plan any actions because we did not have to do anything despite their provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what it says in bullet point 4 where a dead-line is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dead-line? Yes, I can see that. A dead-line was given for those actions to be completed by the 10th of February, 1994. Obviously every time there is a decision, there has to be a dead-line. There was always a struggle with dead-lines and other things as well, but the timing was one of the key factors. And in this case the dead-line was the 10th of February, and from then on, we were supposed to monitor the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps envisage, order, and carry out the opening of fire by heavy artillery between the 4th of February and 10th February 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, it did not. We did not open fire. I know I am a witness, an eye-witness to the developments that took place during that period of time. I know how people perceived the whole situation. They rejoiced at an opportunity to have a peaceful period. Nobody was keen on opening fire, on provoking the enemy, or responding to their provocations. In other words, we did not do anything. It was a period of relief. We reinforced our positions and we arranged our own positions in accordance with the circumstances that prevailed at the time. We didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2807, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D7504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report somebody signed on your behalf, as we will see on the last page. This was issued on the 1st of July, 1994. And now can we go to the last page which is page 2. Thank you. And now could you please read bullet point 8 for us, conclusions, forecasts, and decisions for further action. Can we scroll down in Serbian and can we display bullet point 8 in the English version. Maybe you can tell us in a nutshell what your forecasts were and what you decided.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case we're talking about 1994 and the period is during the month of August. For us that period was when we had obtained conclusive information that the 1st Corps of the BiH army was increasing in the number of troops and the number of weaponry. I believe that I already said that they had started changing the strategy of their use and that strategy of use could be explained by a saying: You don't open a tin from the inside but from the outside. And that referred to Sarajevo, obviously. That practice, that option, was an infernal machine which imposed on us the need to organise ourselves. Actually, they launched attacks from the outside in the direction of Sarajevo, but nobody reacted. Nobody said that for that side, for that type of action, the same decision on a cease-fire should be applied. When it comes to the cease-fire, the only thing that mattered was what was going on in Sarajevo; and as to what was going on outside Sarajevo, that didn't really matter. They used strong forces to attack from the outside and threaten us in Sarajevo. And our attempts to match that caused us major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the following paragraph you say what should be done. You say that the cease-fire had to be respected and that lines should be held firmly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2808, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I believe that last week we discussed the types and manners the 1st Division acted from the city and from outside of the city. Could you please tell us what were the effects of the activities of the 1st Corps of the BiH army and primarily that applies to our troops and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of indicators which were to say that those activities -- and if we're talking about the military side, i.e., about the combatants and units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, we had a lot of problems because of the threats to the civilian population. To be more specific, the area and the people who were living in Nedzarici, a soldier knows how to protect himself in a trench or in a building or behind a wall or behind an obstacle and so on and so forth. Civilians, on the other hand, don't know how to do that, they can't do that. The following locality of that kind is Lukavica. It was the workers' quarters or the workers' neighbourhood very close to the Energoinvest building. We're talking about wooden houses where people could not protect themselves although they were exposed to fire. Another neighbourhood that we called Trapare because all the families there bore the same family name, Trapare, that was a group of houses and people there were like clay pigeons. Vogosca was under the constant fire of the artillery of the 12th Division. Rajlovac as well. Ilijas was under fire that was like hell to them. Every day in Ilijas there were as many as four civilian casualties up to 12 soldiers who were killed, but they were killed in combat, whereas the civilians got killed in the street or in their homes. I don't know whether I am making myself clear enough. I only know that those were difficult situations that had is to be borne, that people had to be protected, that solutions had to be sought in order to open fire to curb their fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just now you told us about this loss of 12 soldiers and daily losses of four civilians in Ilijas. Could you recall some incidents involving major civilian losses as a result of action by the 1st Division [as interpreted] of the BH army, starting with the neighbourhood of Hadzici, Blazuj, Ilidza, Vojkovici, up to Rajlovac, Vogosca, and Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, Dr. Karadzic said "corps" rather than "division" of the BH army at line 25.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but I have to explain. The 14th Division of the 1st Corps was active in Hadzici, and in Ilijas it was the 16th Division, so that the entire corps was firing upon the Serbian part of Sarajevo. The 12th Division was opening fire from the city itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we are now entering the region where there is some doubt as to the relevance. While we understand that it was during the war, please bear in mind you were indicted for specific allegations. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, thank you. I will follow that, but the last sentence by General Milosevic, solutions had to be sought in order to open fire to curb their fire, that means our fire is directly linked to their fire and that is why I wanted to get Mr. Milosevic to recall examples when he was not able to contain anymore and return fire with consequences that were disastrous to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But your question was a bit much broader than this. Please continue. What is your question for the General?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still remember today some drastic examples of our losses that dictated our responding with fire to their fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moments of that kind and that nature were more than one - I cannot enumerate them all now. And I suppose you want to hear about what was going on in the urban part of Sarajevo, not in Nisici and Trnovo areas because there were other incidents there where we had to look for solutions. I know very well in the month of May 1995 unit commanders were reporting that they were under heavy fire. The positions of troops are covered with strong fire and the fire is spreading to civilian areas. My response was to get to the procedure to see whether it was reliably established from where the fire is coming, from which weapons, and to what extent we would be threatening civilians if we responded. That was time-consuming. The second thing I had to do was to inform UNPROFOR to enable them to see what was going on exactly. All this required time and in the meantime my subordinate commanders were very unhappy that I was not giving them permission to respond with fire. I know and I found it somewhere in the papers later, that the UNPROFOR observer was observing this and could see how strong the fire was opened by the 12th Division. That is one thing. Second, we also established that the localities where we could respond with fire would not hurt anyone but the shooters. That was the situation in May 1995. In one of their reports that I saw later, they say that they had engaged in a three-day action, the commander of the 12th Division is reporting to his superior that he had used up all the ammunition and he's asking for new ammunition, and those were thousands of destructive projectiles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter 12388.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One of your reports from 1993, a regular combat report. Page 2 in Serbian. It's probably page 3 in English. Item 8. General, sir, could you read out aloud this passage that says: "In view of the frequency ..." You signed this on behalf of General Galic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read out loud the entire paragraph that begins with: "Given the frequency ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Given the frequency of enemy operations, we foresee that certain units will not be able to tolerate the consequences of enemy fire and consequently will be forced to return fire to protect their personnel. For this reason, a vigorous protest should be made at the fire the enemy is launching from the city. UNPROFOR should take a firmer stand in protection of our units and population." I don't know what kind of comment you expect me to make, but that was our experience, that the fire was going to be only stronger and stronger and that we must protect our personnel and population, and we must also ask for UNPROFOR's assistance, to put pressure on the enemy side just as they were putting pressure on us to contain all types of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that the enemy should be prevented from opening fire from the urban area. You consider all the other fire to be legitimate; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We need to clarify this. There is no such thing as legitimate or illegitimate. You can fire on the enemy as long as it's only the enemy and his weapons. I did not want to observe any other rules and look at nuances such as whether there would be more damage or less damage. If fire was opened by a weapon or a group of weapons or by an enemy unit, we can open fire at them. We could not make any other calculations and take the risk of causing damage to others. I don't know if you understood what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2809, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, while you were still in the 1st Romanija, what kind of orders did you get from the corps command regarding action targeting the city? What was the position of the command? Especially with regard to larger calibres.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question perfectly well. I want to answer as follows. General Galic, who was the corps commander, was far more restrictive and strict than what I am describing. I take my hat off to him, and I can say I have learned from him a lot in terms of how strict you have to be in restricting behaviour that is not legitimate in combat. In other words, not even his predecessor, Sipcic, had a different approach. He was only less demanding. But Galic constantly issued warnings and orders and really insisted with commanders that they must not engage in such behaviour. And that was an encouragement to me to continue in the same vein and only our styles differ.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D3441. The English version is all right. The Serbian is something else. But it's the same date, 31st October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I read this to you in English, General? It will be interpreted to you. 31st October 1992. [In English] "To: All SRK units. "Beginning on 1st of November, 1992, until further notice, it is strictly forbidden to use weapons with a calibre greater than 12.7-millimetres without the permission of the Corps Commander or his deputy. "Deputy commander ... Marcetic." [Interpretation] Did your brigade receive this order and is this consistent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this order, and of course, since I remember it, we received it and I'm aware of it. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher give the General a hard copy in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's no problem. [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] I can only confirm that this is correct and this was a regulation issued by the corps command, and of course it says that this is a ban on the use of calibres greater than 12.7 millimetres. It's all types of mortars, artillery, anti-aircraft machine-guns, guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you understand from this document that any shells that were fired from the Serb side and that were greater than 12.7 millimetre in calibre were fired with the permission of the corps commander, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not the position. The commander made his position known and it was abided by. So irrespective of the fact whether a fighter awaited the commander's approval or not, he had to rely on the clear decision not to engage. In situations when there was no strict prohibition, the fighter in question had to involve the procedure which I have referred to a number of times here, which means that it required full analysis. The brigade commanders who, within the system of authority, certain powers were delegated to, they could act in accordance with certain prearranged decisions if there was a sufficient degree of threat. Their decisions were the same as if they had been received from the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2810, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we next have 1D7509.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, we'll see on the next page -- well, perhaps we can go to that page immediately. It is your document as the Chief of Staff dated the 20th of October, 1993. Item 2, please, "our defence lines ..." Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go back to page 1, please, item 2. We can see it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is stated there about the defence lines as well as response to enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position was as stated here. The defence lines remained unchanged. This was a report. Since there were attempts to attack, our defence stood ground and there were no changes in terms of our forces being pushed back. However, irrespective of the degree of our protection, the units were still cautioned not to open fire on the central part of town, on Sarajevo. There was always a need to be aware of movements and goings-on in Sarajevo because it was an important issue. In Sarajevo, international activity took place as well. That is why there was an order that no fire should be opened even if we were threatened directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the document say about observation and surveillance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, surveillance is a separate profession, so to say. It always had to be in place and all movements had to be observed. I don't think it requires any additional explanation, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The third page of the B/C/S version is nothing to do with the document, so we'll admit only two pages. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2811, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, could we cast a glance on D2567. It is a short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it is an order to all brigades, regiments, and independent battalions dated the 22nd of May, 1993. Some consequences are referred to following the activity of the other side, but irrespective of that, General Galic - and it was Sladoje who issued this on his behalf, I presume - prohibited the firing of any weapons larger than 12.7-millimetre calibre and requires that all means of firing be put under control. Can you recall what consequences are referred to on the 22nd of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. Unless I'm mistaken, I wasn't in the corps at the time, in May 1993. I can confirm, though, that this is a normal standard request or caution stating what is to be done. As far as I know, I was still not with the corps at the time. This strikes me as a normal, regular order referring to certain events which had preceded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in the brigade. It is addressed to all the brigades. Does it mean that the 1st Romanija Brigade received it as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the brigade at that time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, we can have a break whenever you wish to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Could we have a Prosecution exhibit, the number is P01641.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you familiar with this document? Perhaps we can see the other page too. Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 1, please. The first paragraph, can you explain this proposal for setting artillery aside. Why did you send this proposal and what were the reasons that guided you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my proposal and I see it as such. It was my estimate that it was up to me to propose this, whereas the decision was to be made by those whom I addressed, that is to say, the Main Staff. I'm familiar with this document. It was to the effect that a manoeuvre should be made to keep some of the pieces, and I am not trying to hide that. It is true that I proposed it as such. It was all based on my experience until then with the way the war was going on and in light of our co-operation with UNPROFOR. When the decision was made to withdraw the weapons, it was my conclusion that all of our weapons were to be withdrawn and its use restricted, whereas the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, their 1st Corps, had such weapons which even when withdrawn had the range and possibility to be used against the area that was supposed to be under prohibition, the area where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had its lines of defence. If they had the so-called NORAs, that is to say, 155-millimetre howitzers which could reach as far as 32 kilometres, it was all the same to them whether the pieces would be at a permitted location or a location that was not permitted. They were still within the range where they could open fire. That is what guided me to propose to my superior command that a contingent of weapons should be retained as a floodgate, as a means of protection in those circumstances when we were under threat. Of course, I am by the same token not saying that it was the wisest thing to do on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you proposed this based on your previous experience. What was that experience that drove you to proposing this? What was the nature of that experience?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is already 1994 and there was plenty of experience. There were continuing warnings and assertions that we opened fire, whereas allegedly the other side did not. And we all know from practice that they did. Next, the weapons and measures that were supposed to take place were not to be implemented the way as envisaged by the negotiator or whoever accepted this decision, and we knew it would be like that. They hid their pieces in tunnels or other places of low visibility, and UNPROFOR did not see them. I know and I believe that UNPROFOR did see those weapons, but there was no pressure or reason enough to indeed have those weapons truly moved out of their range or stop from being active.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was the cease-fire implemented? Were there violations of cease-fire before and after this date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the cease-fire, well, it's something -- but before I answer let me add this: It was our decision to have a full record of how the cease-fire was honoured by the other side. We knew what we were doing, of course, and it was our decision not to use those means and not to violate the cease-fire. The register of violations of the terms is quite long. I know it's somewhere out there because we created it, and it follows from one day to the next their violations and the characteristics of their activities. We used it as an indicator to show that all agreements and decisions were in vain when they kept being active from one day to the next and violated the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the agreement of the 18th of February, that is to say, one week later, was this proposal of yours adopted? Was it made part of the agreement or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I don't have any regrets. I know that there were people who wanted to observe this, those who were in charge of implementing that decision, and those people did it. All the assets were moved to Krivoglavci, Poljane [phoen], and so on and so forth, as agreed. I was personally there when those things were happening, the assets were being brought over, and the UNPROFOR deployed Bruno's elements, fenced those assets off, and they could no longer be used. I was there when General Soubirou was there and I saw in him a firm position that we were supposed to observe because it was well sounded. The General did not want to greet me. I did not hold it against him. I saw that he was an honest man doing an honest job in order to stop the conflict. My conclusion was that that was his decision; however, once the assets were fenced off, fire was opened from their assets on us - I don't know where they were fenced off, whether they were fenced off at all, who controlled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you mentioned that after that, or rather, that you kept records on the violations of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7033. I am not tendering the previous one because it has already been admitted into evidence. 1D7033.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the record of truce violations starting with the 10th February? And that date is also the date of your previous document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the record. I'm sorry that the letters are a bit small, but I'm sure you can follow the dates, the places, the times when those truce violations happened. You can see when fire was opened as a result of the fact that the 1st Corps did not observe the cease-fire. We monitored those things continuously, not only on those dates, but even later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the precision of the record, 9.15, 8.45, was that a task? Does this truly reflect the times when fire was indeed opened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, where there is a will to have certain information, then that information has to be complete, not only as regards the date but also the time. So we wanted to be perfect in recording those incidents. I dare say that we were even overzealous, maybe we even over-recorded things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would like to tender the whole document, could you put some overall foundation as well as some content of it. The last part of document seems to be of different format. Probably we need some further explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can go to the last page, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, something has been added by hand, 88 times. What is this and why has the structure of the record been altered here? What is this about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Serbian version be zoomed in for the benefit of the General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not necessary. It's big enough. I can't say yes. I don't know -- well, I personally cannot tell you what the difference is between the beginning of the record of truce violations and what I see here now. The format is changed. The columns have been changed. What is missing is the hour when a truce violation happened, but the gist is the same, the number of shells, the time, where, in what area, and what our response was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. Did I understand you properly when you said that the format has been changed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the form, the format has been changed, nothing else. The only thing that is missing are the hours, for example, that things happened at 9.00 a.m. or 9.00 p.m., but the date remains as well as the type of fire which was opened on that particular day and how we responded to that kind of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the last column, whether it was responded, is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whether it was responded or not, yes, which means that the words "yes" and "no" provides the answer to everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you here. Can we see the B/C/S page 31, in English page 55. This is the last page of the first format. Could you see the date, General? That's -- I think it's sometime in April 1994. Do you agree? 30th of April, 1994. And shall we see the next page in the B/C/S while remaining on the same page in English but the bottom of the page. From April it says it's sometime in November. November in what year? Would you like to see the previous page again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what is missing here is the year, the year. Probably the record-keeper, the person who collected this information, he probably thought that the year could be only the year when those conflicts were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is a year. There must be a date containing the year. During the night between the 11th and 12th November 1999 [as interpreted], the enemy opened fire on all the front lines in the direction of Olovo and Kladanj, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it was 1994, would it mean that there was no violation of truce between May and October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that wouldn't mean that. Perhaps no information was collected, perhaps no record was established to that fact. If the information was not complete, it was not entered. If the record was not made, if the note was not made on the day when fire was opened, then it was not registered post festum, after the event, based on memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, having seen part of this document, do you know who produced this document and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was compiled by the operative organ of the command of the 4th Corps [as interpreted]. This means that it was compiled by the operatives who were officers in charge of receiving information, analysing it, reporting to the commander or the Chief of Staff about the developments, and then came up with the analysis that served as our base for future contacts and work with the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you say "4th Corps," "command of the 4th Corps"? I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I could not have said the 4th Corps. I only said the corps command and what I meant was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 3 was admitted previously with Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. Shall we admit them in its entirety? Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no problem with it coming in in its entirety now, Your Honour, given the General's explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the court deputy could remind us of the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Exhibit D2803.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. And now I would like to call up P2420.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, take a look at the document. Tell us whether you remember the document and its contents. Lieutenant-Colonel Sehovac forwarded, and I mean literally, the contents of a telegram he received from the Main Staff. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be shown the signatures. Okay. Thank you. I would have a lot of to say about this document; however, it seems superfluous for me to say anything. This is information that reached General Mladic - I don't know how, in what ways - and then General Mladic issued some sort of a warning not to do what is outlined in the context as something that was being planned. First of all, without going any further into the details of this issue, because this would be out of my character, I'm wondering how come that General Mladic sent a piece of paper like this to Colonel Sehovac as a brigade commander. What he wants to forbid or what he wants to warn about, what he wants to prevent, I commend him for that but he should have done it directly with the corps command or the corps commander. In this case, it seems to me that somebody wanted to invent things and a plot against Mladic wanted him to issue the warning. I don't know whether it was a form of self protection, but in any case there is no action that was ever followed that might prove that any kind of intention on the part of the corps commander ever existed to that effect. It says here that the corps commander held a meeting with civilian structures. First of all, I never held any meetings with the civilian structures. If I had, then we only talked about bringing units to strength. I never discussed combat activities with anybody. For me this is incorrect information, this is superfluous information, and this is what I claim. A meeting of that kind absolutely never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of orders did you issue with regard to fire being opened on town, were they similar to what it says here or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what it says here. The orders that were issued, the measures that were undertaken, I have already described and explained. Any kind of new approvals, any kind of changes in the position or conduct or giving permit to anybody to open unlawful fire on the city of Sarajevo and its citizens, I never issued any such orders. No such orders should have been issued at all in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here somebody forwarded information to Mladic about that meeting that took place on the 5th of November, 1994. Can we see what happened a week earlier on the 27th of October. I'm calling up your document 65 ter 20823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, General, could you tell us what brigade was Mr. Sehovac commander of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, he was commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, Light Brigade, because it did not have a large number of personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 20823.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, first of all, could you look at the second paragraph. "Since our enemy is not abiding by any rules or principles, although we have tried so far to obey -- to observe all the Geneva Conventions until now, as well as direct our actions exclusively towards military targets, if the enemy continues in this way, they will force us to respond as of today to every bullet fired at the Serbian settlement by firing at the selected target under the Muslim control in Sarajevo." And then look in the last paragraph. It says: "Brigade commanders, immediately inform the UN monitors in your area of responsibility about this warning ... never open fire first." And now tell us what you ordered in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We bear great responsibility for saving the Serbian people from the born-again Islamic fanatics. In doing that, we should remain energetic and persistent and humane above all. With that aim, I forbid perfidious killing, wounding, or capturing, and other actions which are not in accordance with the international law of war and the Geneva Conventions." This is just the reiteration of previously stated positions and commitments. This is not a watershed, this is not a change in our conduct. I'm saying that regardless of whether their fire is selective or restricted or not, whether we are in too great a danger, there is no chance that we will cross the Rubicon and do things against the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2812, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the stance of superior commands, that is to say, the Main Staff, relevant to your orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope this will not sound too frivolous, take this with a certain reservation, I would say that you were really nagging us. My fighters and I wondered: Why do you keep cautioning us? We know that. We have nothing to do with any other structures, apart from military structures, the man wielding a gun and opening fire. Your warnings and the warnings we received from the politicians and the Main Staff were so persistent that I understood it as keeping pressure on us so that we would never take any action that would threaten the civilian population in Sarajevo. I respect that. We received those warnings regularly. We also received certain warnings that I liked. I liked them as an expression of a humane approach towards events. We don't want to destroy anyone. We don't want to carry a victory against anyone. We don't want to harm anyone. And whatever is to happen is to happen in a military joust, on the battle-field. In addition, I can say that my brigade commanders shared this feeling and this commitment that we can only engage in military rivalry. Anything else would be a pyrrhic [Realtime transcript read in error "puric"] victory. That was out of the question. We could not carry a victory if we opened fire against civilians because civilians were not our enemies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the Prosecution Exhibit P5642.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your conversation with General Mladic intercepted by the other side. Page 4, please. The date is 16 June 1995. What were the military circumstances on that day, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the night between the 15th and the 16th June 1995, I recall everybody who was there and still alive. I remember that very strong forces moved against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, both from Sarajevo and the surrounding theatre. They were advancing towards us and our civilian population. It was the beginning of an offensive that had been planned by the Supreme Command and the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to, as they called it, lift the blockade of Sarajevo. If -- or, rather, we knew very well what they had planned, what forces they had prepared, in which direction they are moving, et cetera, because they had brought forces earlier on from Fojnica and other places and they wanted to launch this offensive a bit later. But when they saw the unrest among their troops, even we could hear the exchanges of fire from their areas. We knew exactly what needed to be done and what needed to be organised. I made a decision, together with my brigade commanders, how to deploy our forces and to fortify ourselves to repel that offensive. They selected renowned commanders. Famous General Alagic commanded the 7th Corps and we felt the full force of their strike. They came in waves. They sent one contingent of forces into an assault, and when they are repelled, they sent another wave. They kept trying to break out through our positions. They failed. I reported to the Main Staff, to General Mladic, our command, what was being prepared in the night between the 15th and the 16th, and he's asking here how things are coming along. And I tell him: Everything is coming along as I had reported to you earlier, the same scenario. He was fully informed by that time. He needed to ask no questions. He could get his written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle he says: "That is the method. Hold on. Congratulations. I hear you've inflicted major losses on them." Is it true that you inflicted major losses on them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said what kind of operations they mounted and how they employed their units. When one contingent of forces fails to break through, they bring them back and have them rest and then they send another wave. Why they did that and why they used their personnel in that way, I don't know and I don't want to go into that; but we did inflict losses on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further down below it says Mladic says: "They are moving at all costs." I'm not sure this is correctly translated. [In English] "They're fighting tooth and nail and they should be made to pay for it." [Interpretation] What does it mean, that they are going forward at all costs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything unclear here. He has information that they are going for a breakthrough at all costs and that's the only thing he can mean. Their idea was to solve the situation. Ratko Mladic must have meant the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I only meant the area where these forces under the command of Alagic and the other generals were marching towards our front line. They did, they were going for it at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And further down he says: "One by one, destroy, attack, only military targets!" You say: "What?" Mladic says: "Only military targets ..." Was this something new? Was there complete agreement between you and the Main Staff regarding military targets?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was absolute. I am not aware of any waverings, any vacillation regarding the principal decision how to wage this war. There was no change of position, no change of approach. On the contrary, we were completely in agreement - I believe that's clear. We also agreed that we should target only military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, how long did this offensive in the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps last in June 1995, beginning with June 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ran its course. They must have made assessments of what they have managed to do. There must have been subsequent decisions to change axes of attack, change tactics, et cetera. This offensive lasted the whole month of June and July, with varying intensity, and they kept trying to harmonize the action from Sarajevo with the action of the forces that came from a completely different territory, the forces of the 1st Corps that were outside. That was a constant problem for them. Now, look, that is the situation, if you allow me, Your Honours, to present this situation to the Chamber. We had come to a conclusion, we made the estimate that in this overall restructuring of axes of attack, they decided, from the area of Sirokaca, which is just under Trebevic, Mount Trebevic, and from the area of Mojmilo hill, to encircle Grbavica and part of Lukavica. That was felt. I have to add - and this is intended for everyone, primarily to me - that we could not sit on our hands. We had to do something to prevent that. And only thanks to our efforts would the population in Grbavica and other areas be saved. The population addressed us frequently through their delegations, they made requests, they pled with us to provide them with protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said something about their losses. What losses did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps suffer through this sustained offensive and what were the civilian casualties, if any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 7th Corps moved towards the forces of the Igman Brigade, the first losses we had on that axis, that is, the sector and the village of Vela, the territory of Hadzici municipality, in this first wave of attack their battalion commander, Captain Bratic, was killed. And then at this very difficult moment that was a harbinger of impending catastrophe, the fighters rose and did not let them succeed in this breakthrough. The next day, on the 17th, they were facing a choice. I don't know who prepared them and who suggested ways in which they should make their break out. That is part of the Russian strategy, actually. But their way was to choose a narrow axis and then spread their positions further on. They chose that axis in the neighbourhood of Ilijas which was partly encircled and under attack from all sides, but this area was a hill. I could not find it on the topographic map, but I found it on another map. It's a hill called Pijesak where they deployed several artillery weapons and more projectiles landed there than on some major cities in the Second World War. In this fighting, which was very dramatic, I could see that the civilian population, the elderly people were coming from their homes to help carry ammunition, to help the fighting men. In that situation, the grandson is getting killed, the grandfather is trying to save him and he gets killed himself. Then the boy's father comes out to save his son and his father and gets killed too. That was a situation when people were dying like flies but they did not let the front line be broken. Then their forces tried another breakthrough in the area of Nabozici [phoen], but we repelled them again. My assistance to those forces was minimal. I sent only one platoon-strong units to help them because I had no more to give. But I was on the spot. It's very embarrassing for me because I'm getting emotional, Your Honours. To that young commander who was 28 years old, Captain Savic, I came there to help him. Those were the losses and our suffering. On the same day, in Ilijas, 48 civilians got killed. Let me not tell you how many people got killed on other axes of attack. But I remember this moment, very dramatic moment, that remains etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One other question regarding that offensive. What forces, which corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did engage the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the Army of BH with all of their assets, the entire corps, that is, including the divisions in the outer area as well as the 12th Division in Sarajevo itself. In addition to those units, from the 1st Corps, there was also the MUP brigade. It was a brigade-strong force amounting to some 7.000 MUP personnel, not in that brigade alone but in total. The special MUP brigade Bosna as well as other special units were engaged too. They call them "special," although I'm not sure how special they were. But we could feel their effect. Next there were also parts of the 2nd Corps of the Army of BH, that is to say, the Tuzla Corps, with the forces that were in contact with us, that is to say, the 101st Olovo Brigade. There were another 2.000 outside the brigade from the 2nd Corps. So that concludes the 2nd Corps. Then the 3rd Corps commanded by General Mahmuljin. In the corps there were between 12- and 18.000 people. There was also a Mujahedin squad of some 800 fighters. The next corps was commanded by the famous General Alagic, the 7th Corps. He brought his corps to the general area of Visoko and Godusa and Fojnicka Reka. His intention was to continue further afield to Sarajevo and via Igman to Trnovo. Then the 4th Corps, but only some of its parts. The 4th Corps was from Konjic, and they only used a part of their forces that were in immediate contact with the rest of the 1st Corps which had its forces at Igman, Treskavica, and Bjelasnica, and the general area of Pazaric. Those were the forces which meant to destroy us, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say the Mujahedin squad of 800, what do you mean by the term "Mujahedin"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly. I know what a Mujahedin is, but I thought it was a matter of common knowledge and understood as such. They were members of units who were foreign nationals or foreign mercenaries. In any case, they were not from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They arrived from certain countries outside Bosnia and Herzegovina and even outside Europe, of course from non-Serb lands. I didn't try to verify their origin, but I know who they were. It wasn't so much the matter of who it was, but what kind of sentiment, what kind of fear the population felt when they heard of them being blood-thirsty. And we had to work on the perception of the population. In any case, the popular image was that of executioners of people who were ready to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Sarajevo Light Unit you mentioned a moment ago, how strong was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Sarajevo Brigade was a small brigade. In total, they had around 1200 people who were registered. In terms of use, one could count up to a maximum of 800 to 1.000 people from the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the corps as a whole, how many people could it engage in June 1995? How many people could be introduced into combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps used all of the people it had, that is to say, the maximum strength or force that existed, including commands, communications personnel, logistics, technical services, et cetera. In total, it was in the area of 18.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
