utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that you were exposed to attacks from -- units from several different corps, what was the situation like in your neighbouring Serb corps? Could they lend you assistance? For example, what was taking place in the Drina Corps area at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do not hold this against me, please. I don't know exactly what the situation was with those corps, not because I didn't want to know, but you have to understand that I was worried with the situation in my corps. I did ask for reinforcements, although I knew that the Drina Corps -- well, it's a different matter, something that occurred afterwards. In any case, it drew the forces of the 2nd Corps of the Army of BH to pull out their forces in that part of the offensive when the situation around Srebrenica arose. In any case, I do know that the corps had their difficulty, their areas of responsibility, and their problems. I also know that General Talic in a private conversation later told me, "Yes, General, I do know that the SRK was in a difficult situation at the time in June, July, and August, but do not forget that we were in the same kind of difficult situation." I told him, "Well, I'll take your word for it, although I don't know what your situation was like."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 1D7510 to see what happened in early August that same year and how the Main Staff sent this order. 1D7510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a very small matter before we go too much further and it's a transcript matter. Page 39, line 8, instead of "puric," p-u-r-i-c, I think the word should read "pyrrhic," p-y-r-r-h-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and there's a handwritten note that the Chief of Staff should draft our order; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The handwritten note.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't read all of it. This is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the part towards the bottom, can you just describe the contents of item 2, what is it that the Main Staff is asking the corps to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I'd like to read it first. What it says is what we could see in earlier notifications, warnings, or orders. There's no particular reason for me to comment upon this. It pertains to certain prohibitions, caution, and the process of decision-making that only military targets could be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about this, we see that observation posts are ordered to be on duty around-the-clock in order to guide artillery and mortar fire, in order to achieve as great effects as possible with the least amount of ammunition. Fire should not be opened on targets which had not been observed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. I can only repeat what was stated in the rule that we had put in place and we honoured it without anyone's caution. It rose out of necessity. One cannot do anything running blind. One needs appropriate information. One couldn't undertake an activity in order to create an impression of strong fire. One gains nothing by that. All of my men needed time to understand that our fire amounted to nothing unless the target is hit. When hitting barriers like a street or something like that, it means nothing unless we hit the target. Collateral casualties were of no effect and only accurate fire should be opened. I demonstrated to my staff in the following way. When I was in the village of Ostojic at the foot of Treskavica, there was a battery from the 1st Corps. They had 105-millimetre pieces attacking the village the whole day and I happened to be there and I told the fighters, "See, no effect," after all that had been done, and they didn't know that all their efforts amounted to very little. We could engage in action only if we wanted to prevent them from having any effect and we could only do that by direct hits. And the observation system was in operation around-the-clock and the rules that applied were always in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your view, how do you see the allegations from the indictment that we opened fire at the city randomly and that we used disproportionate response?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that category of interpretation. Let me address the issue of proportionality first when opening fire. In order for the SRK or anyone else to open fire proportionately on a target, there are rules in place. If there is a target that is actually a battery which would amount to a firing squadron in position of defence, then the target needs to be either neutralised or destroyed. There is a big difference between the two in the amount of ammunition that is to be expended. No matter how well regulated by the rules, there is no complete destruction. It would be a mere chance to have someone destroy another in totality. Such ambition should not be contemplated unless one had very solid protection. We had our ammunition quantities approved in our combat kits and our units were provided with certain quantities of ammunition that the brigade commanders asked for and I was usually chased about by the brigade commanders because they wanted more ammunition. I wasn't trying to shun or run away from the responsibility. I simply had to tell them that we hadn't any more. Any quantity had to be so limited that they had to come up with different solutions and they realised that. So you set a limit to his ammunition quantity and then they cannot engage in any excessive fire or minimum fire. They only fired when they were certain that they would hit the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2813, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, when it comes to neutralisation or destruction, when are you satisfied? What is the difference in the level of use? How do you know when the target was sufficiently destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything can be established. Everything is well-known. First of all, it was not inexperienced people who waged the war or amateurs who didn't know what they were doing. Everything had to be known, everything had to be well ascertained. If a target was hit, it was also neutralised which did not mean that it was completely destroyed, but it was no longer what had happened to that target. The most important thing was that the target was hit. That target could have remained alive because people don't often die from just one bullet. It takes a lot of bullets sometimes and everybody who participated in the war know that. They knew what was happening to us. We knew what was happening to them. And there is a saying that not every bullet hits the target, but it doesn't really make sense. What makes more sense is that not every shell hits the target. What else can I tell you about this term of "neutralisation"? The measure of destruction is something that we did not carry out because it was not -- impossible to implement. Neutralisation means that the target is rendered quiet by our activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If that is achieved with one or two shells, does the shelling continue, General, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A foreign witness, a monitor, I apologise that I cannot quote the page, to my question which was how he knows what terror is and what it is not. He said that one or two shells constitutes terror. When there is a large shelling campaign, it's militarily justified. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the target because you can hit a group of people who have nothing to do with fighting with one shell. If that shell hits them, for them it's more than terror. I'm not talking about that. I could not follow that witness's thesis because when it comes to the use of assets, I'm not talking about them in that way. However, when a target is hit directly, it does not constitute terror. On the contrary, I have failed to mention that sometime in May when my commanders were exposed to fire and they wanted us to curb their artillery fire, we did not respond to their artillery fire. We launched some direct hits and CNN recorded us targeting their bunkers, but that was never aired. Because some people who watched, some viewers, wondered how could you implement such direct hits in order to prevent their fire. We did it because it was a necessity. Later on, people portrayed it -- portrayed those campaigns as our shelling the city. Let me conclude. When you hit a target, then it's not terror.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were hospitalised at the time on the 19th of August; however, your Chief of Staff was there. I am interested in this as an expression of the corps' policy and position. Please look at bullet point 1, where it says that the system of observation should be improved in platoons and battalions and so on and so forth. How does this tally with the policies and position of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its tactics?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fits really well with all that. I've already said I believe that warfare cannot be done by blind people. Every officer and every command as a whole knew how they could organise their defence system, how they could implement their war tactic. I am glad to see that the continuity is very clear. I said it very clear that the continuity starts with the corps commander, who was Galic, then it came down to me. We can see that Colonel Sladoje, who remained in charge of the forces, firstly knew very well what to do; and secondly, he applied the same methods, the same practices, and he had the same demands of his unit. There was no discontinuity there. There were no changes in the policies. There were no changes in conduct. There was no slacking on anybody's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He says here fire has to be planned. And under 3, it says: "In all units, ensure that fire is opened according to plan and that units, adjacent units, and the population are previously informed so as to avoid unnecessary losses when the enemy returns our fire." Could you please tell us what your obligations were vis-a-vis the population that resided close to your assets, i.e., what were your obligations and what was your attitude, i.e., what is implied with bullet point 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not going to say here that we did everything perfectly, a hundred per cent. However, protection measures for civilians were implemented, and the basic measure was not to allow the civilians to remain in the area where there were artillery assets and combat positions. Let's understand each other. The civilians never even tried to find themselves in such areas. The exceptions were those who were carrying ammunition, who moved with the columns. This does not apply to the prevention of their presence there. I am here talking about the exclusion of a civilian population from such areas. We could not implement that by way of moving people physically from the areas of combat activities. We could warn them. And I bear the responsibility for those people in the workers' log cabins near the Energoinvest building and the school of electrical engineering. There were people there. There were no artillery assets there, but those people nevertheless got killed. Men, women, and children got killed by artillery fire particularly during this offensive. I did not issue any decision to move them out because there were no artillery assets there. To be honest, I didn't do anything because I never expected that they could be targeted. And, unfortunately, they got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the following page, bullet point 7. Let's see what Colonel Sladoje ordered. It says here: "Inform the population and prepare it to leave and stay in shelters. Use the police force to prevent the civilians from moving in the area of combat activities and completely stop civilian traffic." Is this in keeping with the commander's obligations towards civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is self-explanatory. This shows clearly what he as commander did. There is no ambiguity here. This is something that he was duty-bound to do and he did it. These are facts that demonstrate that everybody knew what needed to be done to protect people. This is excellent. I think that he did very well here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were the obligations of the officers of the other side with regard to their own civilians and how did they comply with those obligations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is this: I'm not going to discuss their obligations. I believe that they are self-explanatory. They should have known what they were supposed to do. In the overall constellation of relations, we could not seek justifications. We could not say they were duty-bound to protect the area from which they opened fire to move the population out. It was our task to establish whether that area was still inhabited by civilians, and if there were civilians, we should not have opened fire on those areas and we did not. If the area was not cleared, we applied the procedure that I have already mentioned several times. First of all, there would be observation, information would be provided as to what was observed, what kind of assets were there, and then the officer assess their threat, and after that we either used our assets or we prevented their use. It is only normal that they were supposed to protect their own population. They should have disallowed them to remain in the locality where combat activities were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2814, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you mentioned the profitability of a target and the acceptability of collateral damage. How were these things guiding you in your actions? Were those principles your guide-lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very important for any shelling campaign if it was considered that there would be a lot of casualties on our side, the only thing that we did was to carry out the necessary assessment in order to obtain some information. Even if there was a possibility for people to get killed although they were not direct participants in fighting, in order to minimise the collateral damage and to be different than the damage we suffered from their fire, if there were to be losses due to heavy fire from that area, that locality was targeted only if there was minimal collateral damage among civilians and that amounted to one or two people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D8012.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just told us that the number of shells does not have anything to do with the number of victims. Which shell is the most dangerous in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I wonder -- I've just been listening to a couple of different channels of interpretation. I wonder if Dr. Karadzic and General Milosevic could be encouraged just to measure their pace in their questions and answers a little bit so that our colleagues can keep up with the speed of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to make pauses, but I wanted to accomplish as much before our lunch break. You mentioned the fact that the number of casualties does not depend on the number of shells. What happens after the first or the second shell? Which shell is the most dangerous for manpower in their sequence of being fired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us agree on one thing. When I say that the number of shells is not the right measure, I'm talking about our military positions. I am not saying that one, two, or a hundred are perilous if none of them have hit the target. I don't know whether I am making myself clear. I know what I'm trying to say. I'm trying to say that not every shell kills. Shells don't kill people who are protected. This was my intention. I wanted to convey that message to my artillery men. I didn't want them to think that when they launch a great number of shells that they are effective. They're only effective if they hit the target. That's the rule and that's what I tried to convey as a message to my artillerymen. And when we're talking about shells missing targets, nobody knows what the collateral damage will be and nobody knows which one in the sequence will be the most dangerous. The first one is the warning one and every next shell is dangerous. But the first one is the most dangerous because after the first one, everybody tries to find shelter and it is especially dangerous and perilous if it hits the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at what your Chief of Staff wrote on the 30th of August while you were still on sick leave. What he said happened after the alleged Serbian massacre of civilians at Markale. He says that an air-strike started, and in the third paragraph he says that several thousands of projectiles fell, that there was civilian damage in Hadzici, Ilidza, and in the general sector of Lukavica. When you returned from your sick leave, did you get informed about the consequences of that shelling campaign?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th August, yes. I returned to the corps on the 9th or the 10th September, which means ten days later than the events described in the document. Of course they told me what had been going on. Among other things, the corps command had to relocate. It was no longer in the same place where I left it because it was exposed to direct fire, but I would say very sophisticated and very precise fire by rapid action forces from the Mount Igman. Let me not tell you now about this Rapid Action Force. Of course they reported to me and they told me about the aviation attacks, but I also saw some of that action when the bombs fell on an area overlooking Lukavica. And I know why they landed there. There used to be a base for the 247th Self-propelled Rocket Regiment which had moved out of there as early as 1992 and moved to Novi Sad. But their installations remained there and people used that for cover. And the NATO aviation dropped a lot of its load in that area. I was -- I got there early enough to see some of that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop here? What's the relevance of this part?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need two minutes, Your Excellency. Because you will see from further questions that it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two minutes, yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you ask your associates to report to you about the events of the 28th of August and what kind of information did you get about the origin of the shell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask for that and I have to say clearly here I was not aware of the incident. Because I was not aware, I couldn't ask for the information. But they did tell me of their own accord what happened at Markale on the 28th of August. Quite naturally, people told me. They told me that an anathema fell on the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because people said it was their mortar who fired their shell. However, on that day, no such fire was opened, no such shell was used. That is what I heard from Cedo Sladojevic, Colonel Lugonja, and some other officers from the inner circle of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in item 4 it says: "Continue to refrain from opening fire on the city with artillery weapons and do not fire on UNPROFOR personnel and assets."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our continuing position the way we had agreed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 22 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned decision-making procedures. Can you tell me, what was the process of making the decision whether larger calibres will be used? What was the input from the ground and who made the decision ultimately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first requirement that had to be met was to find out whether the target is detected. It was not enough for fire to be observed from that area. It was necessary to narrow down the area, to identify the target, its surroundings, that is to say, its immediate locality. The second thing that needed to be established was the type of weapon, the type of fire, and the number of weapons, whether it's one, two, three, or five guns, and of which calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, whose weapons are you talking about when you say type of weapon and number of weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that was implied. If we are considering and discussing targets, then I'm talking about fire opened by the 1st Corps by their guns, their assets, and the military targets they represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted it to be crystal clear to the participants.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These decisions had to be taken very quickly because action is sometimes pointless if it comes too late. And of course we were not computers. We were not machines to analyse this data very quickly. So the next thing to be considered was the damage that could be inflicted on things other than the target, the surrounding people, buildings, installations, et cetera. We needed information about that from our sources. The commanding officer on the ground had to verify all that and to check if the initial report is really accurate. Sometimes even a trained observer is not always qualified to represent the situation accurately. If we had a target who posed a danger to the forces of the SRK, then we would open fire with the most profitable weapon, such as mortars, or stronger weapons that would enable us to neutralise that target and prevent it from opening fire against us again. Or are you asking me who makes the decision? The brigade commander or even I if I'm there on the spot. If I'm not, then the person whose units are in danger will make that decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 8, next to the word "danger," I should like to add the word "great" because the General said if there is a "great danger" then the fire would be opened. We could hear it on the tapes if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course, I understand that you could make that decision as the highest commander, but what is the lowest level for such decision-making?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not be anyone lower than brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I add this? We are not talking about the urban area. This whole discussion is about the urban area. In other areas I believe it is perfectly clear that our problems were not just in the narrow area of Sarajevo, but the whole broader region. If we are talking about areas outside the city, about clearings, then this decision to open fire could be made by a company commander as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But speaking of the decision to use heavy weapons, what resources did brigades have and what resources did battalions have and what were your orders in that respect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope it is perfectly clear and that detailed explanation is perhaps superfluous, but I'll try. The basic assets used on the targets we discussed before were the assets at the disposal of the brigade command. It could be howitzers, 100-, 105-millimetres mortars, 120-millimetres, and those were the heavy weapons they had. They didn't have any other heavy weapons. The corps artillery had more powerful weapons that were not in use, such as howitzers 155. They were eliminated from use in 1994 when they were withdrawn and placed under the supervision of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Artillery groups, how are they grouped? There were some on the level of brigade, some on battalion level, some on the corps level. Companies did not have them; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, companies could only have 60- and 82-millimetre mortars, but not all companies had them because they had to be scattered over such a large area and not every company commander could have his own artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how about the outside forward line of defence facing the 2nd and 7th Corps and the 14th and 16th Division, how did the line run through populated areas and did you have any restrictions imposed on the use of artillery there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those areas were mostly clear, unpopulated -- mostly unpopulated. However, specifically in the area where the Ilijas Brigade was fighting parts of the 16th Division near Breza and Visoko, they were also in contact with the urban area. It's good that you reminded me about this. There was never a problem if a shell landed in Visoko, but when a shell landed in Sarajevo, then whole world saw it as artillery rampage. They did not respond to action in higher ground. There was always this tendency to concentrate on Sarajevo as a city in danger, and Visoko is also a town just like Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Muslim shells landed in Ilijas, an urban area in Sarajevo, on average during the war? Did you have any sort of records, even rough?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not keep that kind of record. I would take the liberty now of saying that there was too much fire of that kind, but we did not count the shells. That's why I cannot give you a precise number. But I can tell you that Ilijas was under fire, not only artillery fire but also under 12.7-millimetre fire because it was such a compact area. Ilijas was a place that was -- whose surroundings were crawling by all sorts of forces and it was constantly under mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were neighbourhoods like Visoko, Breza, Zupca, a large Muslim concentration, in the range of SRK artillery? Did you target them and did you raze them to the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not impossible to reach. It was not impossible to fire there. I'm talking about Visoko. As for Breza, that locality was far enough to be out of our range.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Zupca, it wasn't far, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually Zupca. As far as I remember, that's a village. It was not too far but it was not under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you remind us, what kind of relationship did Republika Srpska have with Yugoslavia in 1995 at the time of this offensive that three or four corps launched against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? I don't mean the political relationship. I mean trade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I understand. Concerning these specifics, I know there was a decision to impose an embargo on import of assets. This embargo was imposed by Serbia and they banned all deliveries to Republika Srpska of equipment, food, fuel, all sorts of supplies. And I'm trying to tell you and you, Your Honours, I am only aware of this. I've read about it but I did not deal with that directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where did we produce shells in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This production was at the Pretis factory in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did we get steel for these shells?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody else might know that. The situation was like this: The director of that factory was complaining to me that he had no imports, nothing to produce anything with. So by coincidence I went to Ilijas to deal with something else and I saw there the ironworks, the former factory of Ilijas, and I saw behind the factory a huge heap of steel. And I asked if they don't need it to give it to Pretis, but they said it's not the type of steel they need. So I was actually so ignorant about these things that I could not distinguish between what is good for military production and what's not. I was simply barking up the wrong tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to avoid leading questions, but tell us about this embargo imposed by Yugoslavia in 1994. Did it also apply to the steel from Niksic in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that. That was the key product. Looking in hindsight, I realise now that we needed it more than food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to air bombs and that is why I asked about the situation with logistics in the SRK at the time. Do you know whether the Muslim side had or used air bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge and in this case my assertion is that they did have air bombs. To be more precise, around the 18th or perhaps the 22nd of April, 1992, the special forces of MUP commanded by Dragan Vikic entered the Pretis factory and started taking away certain quantities of ammunition and they even took the stock of air bombs that there were in the warehouses. There was a skirmish, a conflict, between those who protected the factory and those forces. And once it was over, some of those assets were taken away. It only confirms that they had a certain amount of air bombs at their disposal. Secondly, I do know, although I'm unaware as to how extensively they used it, they did have an arsenal of anti-aircraft weapons -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry, air lethal assets. The main depot was in Busovaca, which is in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was Croatian territory, to tell you the truth, but how they divided the loot from Busovaca is something I don't know. But they did certainly have preconditions to receive supplies of air bombs. In this particular case, in addition to other lethal assets, air bombs were there as well. And I do know that because I used to command a military police battalion and, as such, I was aware of the situation in each and every warehouse and what was being held where back then in the time of the JNA and in peace time. I stand by my assertion that potentially they did have it at their disposal, but I don't know how diligent they were in keeping matters up-to-date. What I also know is that in the location of the national park at Vrace, there are certain monuments there as well, there were three air bombs that were dropped there but went unexploded. Colonel Cedo Sladoje called me because he was astonished and he wanted to show it to me. He wanted me to see something that on one hand was a dangerous asset for us and, on the other, we were happy that they did not explode. One landed in a civilian's garden and the other two landed in the park itself. We were very happy that they went unexploded. This tells you a lot about whether they did have it or not. If they managed to drop it on our heads, they must have had some.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how they launched them, how were they able to reach Vrace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they launched them. There's nothing else I can say. We all know how they could have launched them, the same way we did. They asserted that alleged bombs came from our side which fell into the Miljacka, and they said they extracted them, used powder for their rifle grenades. But what I actually fear is that they dropped the bombs which they had extracted that way to attack us with them. There was another thing that I wanted to share with the Court. I had information that the person who created those assets to be launched from their side was Mr. Berko Zecevic, who had worked at Pretis, and he had advocated the use of such assets even before. I'm simply sharing the information I had at the time although I'm not claiming anything. I know that he tried to produce such assets even back when he had worked at Pretis. He was competent and intelligent enough to design such an asset which was of significant force, significant power. Also, one needed a level of technical education to have them launched as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, General. Let me ask you another thing about this topic. Were there any classical-type JNA weapons that the SRK or VRS had that the Army of BH did not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the other way around, depending on the type of weapon. I am not discussing the VRS as a whole. I'm only discussing the SRK now. We did not have the NORA howitzers, whereas the 1st Corps of the Army of BH did and the 1st Corps did as a matter of norm, standard. They produced it in the Bratstvo factory and they kept developing them during the war. We did not have that kind of asset. As for the rest we had, they had it too. All of that had come from the same armed force. Both forces were created out of the same basis and we had the same assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to the NORA howitzers, did they have 133-millimetre cannons called Sultan? Did they have such cannons at Igman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was a 130-millimetre gun. It has a long barrel and the calibre was 130. It wasn't as large as you said because I don't think they would have been able to manage such large calibres. As a professional, I'm not even aware of that calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D7031, please. This is the audio recording of the 10th of August, 1995, session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could we have page 7 in the English and we'll move on to page 8, whereas in the Serbian we need page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you suffer the consequences of the attacks of such air bombs even before the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you we suffered no consequences. I simply realised that they had them. Our problem was the dynamics of activities that were underway. It was reported to me literally that some kind of contraption landed in Nedzarici, apparently having large destructive power. To tell you the truth, I had no time to verify at all because combat was of such intensity that we could only establish whether there was any resulting damage to Nedzarici so as to enable a breakthrough on their part; and if that was negative, we no longer bothered. It seems that some kind of contraptions also landed at Ilijas. At times of their aggressive action, we simply did not have time to carry out on-site investigations and keep records. We just moved on. If we could protect ourselves in spite of such danger, we simply continued fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 13 one reads, as you said, that "we were aware that we had them," whereas you say that "we were aware that they had it." Were you aware of the Muslim side having air bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said basically. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read out Silajdzic's reply, the last sentence before the president. He says: "There is some talk of some 26 airplanes that arrived in the last few days. If this refers to about 10.000 multiple rocket-launcher rockets and 10.000 ARPDZ and 800 aerial bombs, et cetera, then I can say if this is about this and this was among other things ..." And then the president says: "This has not arrived yet. We are waiting." And then Silajdzic says: "When I mentioned the four flights, they had already gone by then, which means that stuff was being brought in. If that's what it's about, I can tell you that my sister, our ambassador to Pakistan, procured it. However, she resigned but I took care of the money. So it was paid to them via Malaysia." Did you know that they were buying assets in these far away countries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the rockets mentioned here, that they were used against the units of the SRK. The kind of procedure they had concerning procurement and their connections, that is something I was not aware of. It wasn't within my remit to know. What was much more important for me was that I could feel the impact of such weapons after a wave of additional reinforcement which occurred as of the second half of 1994 and in early 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that the page in English does not correspond to the one in Serbian. Can we have this admitted, Your Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check whether we have correct English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 7 and 8 in English. So the previous page -- the bottom of the previous page in the English. Yes, we see there where it says "800 aerial bombs." And the rest is at the top of page 8. Your Excellency, I seek to tender the entire transcript because we also admitted all other similar Assembly transcripts en bloc, as a whole, a package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the case of Serbian sessions. I'm not sure if we need to admit them all. We'll admit English pages 7 and 8. I think that's sufficient. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually, having read the whole document, I think Your Honours would be better able to understand the context within which the remarks at pages 7 and 8 are placed if you had the whole document. I'm not normally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary you may --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- out to burden the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you may tender it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask -- thank you. May I ask whether the documents of Muslim authorities should be treated as Serbian documents and admitted as a whole so that we could all rely on them during our closing arguments and submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we have aerial bombs? Why did we have them and how did we use them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have aerial bombs. As an asset which proved itself useful. It was something we needed. We were put in a situation where we needed to have more destructive or stronger weapons which would address the situations and circumstances which could not have otherwise been resolved if we wanted to use smaller types of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have these smaller types of weapon in sufficient quantities, such as shells of different calibre that were being produced in the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pretis factory was one thing, whereas the VRS is a much larger entity than the SRK alone. We received some of it from the Pretis company but not enough. It confirms what I said before. The Pretis factory could not produce sufficient quantities because they did not have enough raw materials. We did not have sufficient assets to conduct our defence adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Prosecutor calls those bombs "modified air bombs" in its documents, can you tell us, is it the bomb itself that was modified or is it the way it was launched modified? What was it that was actually modified?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no modifications done to the air bomb in terms of its power, the way it exploded, and so on and so forth. It remains a classical bomb, just as it used to be, and that's as far as the air bomb is concerned. The modification in question and the term that was used had to do with the way it was launched. It was not us who called it a modified aerial bomb. We just called it an aerial bomb. What was modified was the way it was launched. It was no longer thrown from the air. It was launched from the ground from a launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was it launched? What was its fuel? What powered it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if I may be allowed to say something. I went through all of those stages in my case and what arose was a statement that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps actually invented that kind of bomb, that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps used it first, ever. My information is different so I'm going to give you a totally different story. As early as in 1981 or in 1982, I was a battalion commander. I attended a training course after Strela 1, a type of anti-aircraft weapon, was launched. That training took place in Slovenia and we were trained to launch that type of weapon. And then I saw a launcher and a model of an aerial bomb launched from it. The crew was thus trained to use that Strela anti-aircraft weapon. I paid good attention to that Strela weapon and to what we were being told. Unfortunately, I did not pay as much attention to the launcher and the way that asset was fired. It was only later that it occurred to me that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps could not have been a creator of that aerial bomb because that had already been done and tested in other places. And the change consists in the way that bomb was launched, not from the air but from the ground, and it was not our product.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the fuel? What about the way those bombs were fired? What was their nature? How precise they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you everything and I can explain. At the corps command we designated Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Ugresic and we engaged him to be that link. But before that, before that, I have to tell you that the Sarajevo region and the factories in Sarajevo, such as Pretis, Orao, and so on and so forth, they all had purpose production. In that area there was a host of engineers, a host of experts in weapons. They always offered us to improve things or to create things for us. We could not rely on the know-how of those people because they maybe harboured other ideas. That's why the Lieutenant Ugresic was the link between those creative factors, those who were engaged in manufacturing the launcher and mounting the engines to fuel the aerial bomb. A person who was an expert, who was very moderate, very conscientious and diligent, he was vigilant. He monitored their work in order to tell us whether what they were doing could be used or not. He was personally in the testing ground where those assets were tested until they ended up with something that could be used in combat, if you people understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the name of that Lieutenant-Colonel, Milan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ugresic, Ugresic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which rockets, which engines were used to be attached to the air bomb? Did you know? Do you have that technical data?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you who was in charge of that, who was designated to monitor that and to inform us. I cannot repeat the details and the description of those engines that he gave me, their construction and use. As far as I know, those engines were taken from the -- from multi-barrelled rocket-launchers. They were rocket engines. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. KDZ3083 [as interpreted] was a witness here and he testified to the fact that before that aerial bomb was used, it was tested at Zuc. Did you know anything about the testings of that aerial bomb before they finally were used in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, before going further, yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think on this one I'd like to ask Dr. Karadzic for a citation, Your Honour. I think that's a misstatement of the evidence and it's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And it -- what's the witness number again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Something that I think doesn't exist. The translation or the transcript says "3083." That's also what I heard from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "383." I did not mention any 0s. I don't think that he was protected, but I don't want to take any chances with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see that number. Can we get the name, Ms. Edgerton, if he's not protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me just ask, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not exactly -- I have someone in mind, but I'm not exactly sure if it's the same one in Dr. Karadzic's, so I'm not -- perhaps we can rely on the Prosecution for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say. Milomir Soja. I don't think he was protected. If he was, then we need to redact this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he was not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he was number 383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And did you, in the meantime, check the -- check your reference as regards Ms. Edgerton's objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sladojevic is looking for it and he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But even without that, General sir, did you know anything about the accuracy of these assets and the ways the accuracy of those assets was established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ugresic claimed that the experts who worked on those assets practically perfected the weapon to the point at which it could be considered precise. If the target was visible, if the calculations were properly made, that weapon could hit the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript 7217, lines from 16 through 20, Witness Soja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he inform you where those testings had taken place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kalinovik, at a testing ground which is an open space in the direction of Mount Zelengora.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were those bombs fired from? How significant was their precision for your forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those assets were fired from the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That area or that zone is behind the lines of the units which were in their trenches, and if there were residential areas on the axis, those bombs would go across those areas. But those situations were mostly avoided and they chose such localities where such aerial bombs would have to overfly only our units. Those were the circumstances which required caution and it had to be made sure that there was a high degree of precision, otherwise the bomb may have landed on our forces. And let us be clear on one thing. I know that when we're talking about Soja, Soja reported, or rather, I apologise, he testified about some sort of testing and that that aerial bomb fell on a hangar in the territory that was under the control of the VRS. I don't know anything about that period. When it fell over there, all further work was abandoned until conditions were put in place for the electronics to be perfected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many aerial bombs were used in the forward part of defence in the outer ring and how many in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When dealing with aerial bombs, I perceive that question as having its specificities in the following sense and let me tell you what they are. We used two aerial bombs, one in Nisici and the other in Trnovo, in the direction of Treskavica. That was at the time when their offensives were already in full swing. They did not react. They did not say that they had been hit by something, but they were stopped in their advancement. Neither was anybody else interested in the bomb being used in those localities. It was construed as the aerial bombs were something good and not dangerous, and later on, it became the biggest bogeyman for the urban territory. They were used in both areas but not with the same significance. All of a sudden it occurred to somebody to say that that bomb was the biggest bogeyman for the mass murder of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was its precision in Nisici and in Trnovo? Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far are the two locations from the city and in what directions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The locality of Nisici and all the sectors around it are some 40 to 42 kilometres from the city or thereabouts. The same applies, it may be somewhat shorter, towards Trnovo and Treskavica, when the bombs were fired from Trnovo to Treskavica. I can't speak about precision, save for the fact that their attacks were stopped which means that our aerial bomb achieved its goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did the use of those bombs start in the city of Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assessed periods in order to see what kind of combat operations lie ahead of us. We arrived at the assessments that I have mentioned on several occasions. We decide to opt for a new strategy and for reinforcement. We saw that they opened fire from out of the city because they had concluded that they were less successful in trying to break through from the city. And that's why we started coming up with reinforcement in order to stop their onslaught from those axes. The situation was well assessed; however, what happened next was not based only on those assessments. When they got reinforcement and -- during the offensives, they became very efficient and they could break out from the city of Sarajevo. The 12th Division had grown to such proportions in terms of manpower and equipment that we realised that we needed to open fire on those forces that were breaking through from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In my indictment I am charged with an incident which happened on the 24th of May, 1995, in Safeta Zajke Street. Allegedly 100 -- a bomb fell 100 metres away from the industrial compound, i.e., from the wire. It is said that two people were killed. Do you recall the circumstances of that date, 24 May, and the incident in the Safet Zajke Street, I believe it used to be called Drinska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing that I don't remember if it has to do with military operations and developments in that period and especially in that locality. When we'd get information that they concentrated certain weapons and especially 120-millimetre mortars, because in this case we are discussing they were attempting to cut off our road from Lukavica to Pale through Trebevic in a place called Zlatiste, near that feature. They did it in such a co-ordinated way that they were attacking on one axis with weapons and in another area they were preparing a breakthrough towards Nedzarici. Now, concerning this incident in - what's the name of that street? - Safet Zajke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where they had six 120-millimetre mortars covering Nedzarici and part of Ilidza with strong artillery fire, and they brought their forces close to the Stupsko Brdo area so that after that artillery attack, their infantry could move in. With the air bomb we stopped them at Safet Zajke Street and neutralised those six mortars, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of their operations do you recall on the 24th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that they were trying to mount these offensives, but it turned out that these operations of theirs - I cannot now find a good word for it to explain - but that made it clear to us that they were trying to change the whole course of the war. Our response to this fierce attack was again seen as us endangering Sarajevo and very soon afterwards NATO air-strikes began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the 25th of May, right, not August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, May. We're not discussing August now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same indictment concerning the same day, 24th of May, I am charged with the incident in Majdanska Street, where allegedly an air bomb flew into a residential area killing two and wounding six. Can you tell us, was that street also engulfed in the offensive and what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is the same locality, parts of Novo Sarajevo, from which they launched their operations with the proviso that this area, Majdanska Street, territorially belongs to the 101st Mountain Brigade. And their forces attempting a breakthrough went through the well-known Ozrenska Street, that's the street which leads to Majdanska, and their forces were trying to cut off that Ozrenska Street. And this Ozrenska Street is like a knife's edge. Whoever manages to get to the south side has made it; we no longer have a chance to stop them. So they were attacking with mortars from that locality. I know that their air bomb landed in a certain place killing nobody. I know from their reports. The indictment says otherwise, that it killed people. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, G-11 in the indictment only refers to a missile projectile. Is it your or Prosecution's case that the bomb landed in this Safeta Zajke on the 24th of May was indeed a modified aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I was not clear enough before. This one in Majdanska Street hit a transformer station. The closest residential building was a hundred metres away. Do you believe that it was a legitimate hit, in view of the precision of air bombs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to assert anything because I don't know how the Court will understand whatever I say. I know that we were targeting a position that posed a danger to us, and that is how I see it and that's why I estimate that it was justified to neutralise that fire. As for the distance, 130 metres or 140 metres to the residential building, I still believe that it was far enough to be safe. It cannot be damaged by our action. Of course people will be unhappy about it, but there are no casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, the indictment states that in Safeta Hadzica Street a bomb landed, two people were killed and 12 were -- sorry, two people were seriously wounded and 12 lightly injured. What was the purpose of firing that projectile? Was it still during the Muslim army offensive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll first answer about the offensive. It's impossible that we would have fired if everything was quiet and nobody was attacking us. In that incident, what I know and what I recollect and what the reports that reached me said, fresh forces had been brought in to attempt a breakthrough. They were trying and they had the firm intention to link up with 104th Brigade through Nedzarici and that reinforcement they had brought was about battalion strength and they were in the expecting sector. And it was clear their intention was to bring in that reinforcement for attack in the sector, in the expecting sector, of the brought-in battalion which had about 600 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Concerning the 16th of June, what was the situation in the Sarajevo theatre on that day, 16 June 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have already discussed this date, going through the intercept with General Mladic. I provided information and explanation that the well-known Tehber offensive had commenced. It was a situation from which we had to find a way out. Now, the 16th of June -- I know all these situations here, but speaking about the 16th of June, the air bomb that is said to have been fired at Dositejeva Street in the centre of Sarajevo, I know that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not do that and it was not its air bomb, if it had been fired at all. The same applies to the street, although it doesn't feature in your case, called Cobanija, formerly Masarykova Street. They claim that one of our air bombs fell there, damaging, hitting, part of a boiler room. Now, as for the Dositejeva Street, it destroyed a toilet. And they claimed it destroyed five businesses. How can anyone claim that because it's the heart of Sarajevo? There could not have been five small shops there. Anyway, I assert that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not fire these bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know of any military target in Dositejeva Street, regardless of whether it was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that fired or not or whether there had been a bomb all? Were there any military targets there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say before that I knew everything, but, of course, there may have been things I didn't know. I knew about Dositejeva Street that the 1st Corps command is headquartered in the vicinity. I knew that there were people -- the crew of chopper squadron, I received a report about that, that they had their residence there, but I did not go there to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The indictment alleges that three people were lightly injured. What kind of damage would you expect if that place had really been hit by an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I'm saying, if it had indeed fallen there, it must have caused much greater destruction. And if it caused no destruction at all, then I wonder what this is all about. This incident was mentioned in my trial too. Not a single witness was brought to testify about that incident, to say yes or nay. Mr. Berko Zecevic spoke about this. One of the first allegations of the investigative organs was that the air bomb was fired from the area of Pionirska Dolina, and if you fired anything from that place, you would hit several high-rises before getting to Dositejeva. But then Berko Zecevic comes and says: No, it was fired from the Pretis factory. So there are different versions. In my mind it was neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of June the indictment states that our air bomb hit the Square of International Friendship - you will tell me which brigade's area that was - lightly injuring seven people. Part of what military operations was this and whose area was this Square of International Friendship?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that it was the area of responsibility of the 102nd Mountain Brigade which had direct contact and was jointly attacked with this battalion of ours and was attacking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- our battalion in Nedzarici and again this was an attempt to stop their attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand you have reservations about the number of casualties in one incident. Even the indictment says that the total number of casualties, the total number of people killed by this air bomb was five. How do you see that and what does it look like to you from the viewpoint of international law of warfare? Even if we had done all that, even if we were responsible, what do you say about five people being the total of casualties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of law, I'm not saying that five people killed is nothing. That's a lot. That's one thing. Two, if they were portraying this image of a hugely destructive weapon, then this number would seem to indicate that it isn't. But with a good selection of target and precision of fire, it is possible to avoid civilian casualties if you target only militaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that a major offensive was underway at the time of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very clearly, the enemy was engaging a huge force in order to solve their problem and their problem was to how to create this space for linking up, for further integration and unification of Bosnia as they saw it under their control. I didn't want to go into whether their plans were realistic or nonrealistic. But in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, everyone to -- down to the last man was determined to protect their own homes and their areas. In the end, of course, they had to leave or they were driven out, but still they were happy that they were not militarily defeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the schedule number that happened on 16th of June at the Square of International Friendship? Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's G-15, and of course the number of victims is seven lightly injured and not five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it talk about any killed persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I did not count the wounded, but there were five killed people in all of the incidents put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I understood, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Finally, at first instance of use of an aerial bomb in the area of responsibility of the SRK and in the town itself took place on the 7th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that -- to that end, let's look at P01201.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if Dr. Karadzic can rephrase that question, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was interpreting the indictment, Your Excellency. In my indictment, the incident is referred to under that date, so I am pursuing the allegations in my line of questioning. But if you wish, we may well continue this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you take a look, what paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: G-10, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to ask the last question for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, only this: Do you recognise this document and can you tell us why you issued the order? What were the circumstances? What were the circumstances of issuing the order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have explained in my prior testimony what kind of events, activities, and actions there were in the area of Hrasnica, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Butmir. The Ilidza Brigade, in the area they defended, were constantly under fire from the forces at Hrasnica. They were under threat of extermination of all soldiers and civilians. The area defended by the 2nd Sarajevo Unit at Grlica, Vojkovici, and the area towards Lukavica was attacked even more fiercely. If need be, I am ready to show how active they were in the area. All of the weapons that were supposed to enter Sarajevo were held there. The weapons arrived across Igman where there was a selection made and then they kept much of the good pieces. The 104th Motorised Brigade, for instance, it was the ringleader, I would say, and dealt unfairly even vis-a-vis its superiors. They didn't care about anyone. They were more extremist and they were busy with that rather than trying to make a breakthrough. They usually took it out on our civilian population. That was one thing. Another thing, weapons were arriving through that area, units were leaving, deploying themselves in Niksici and Trnovo, it was a military space boiling with a number of soldiers, activity, attacks on the engine factory, et cetera. When my subordinates told me that it became unbearable to sustain any further fire from certain locations at Hrasnica - there was mortar fire and ZIS cannons of 76 millimetres - they suggested that we should use an aerial bomb. I decided so. I used it. But first I asked them to pin-point a target, which would make sure that their attacks ceased or were reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what the first paragraph refers to. There seems to have been an attack underway for three days in the Famos factory area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The text speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, this has already been admitted as a P exhibit and we may conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of January, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
